title: Wyckoff Spring
teaches: The Wyckoff spring as we teach it: in a leader above its 200-day, resting in a flat sideways range, price dips a little under the floor and closes back inside. We read the range, the depth of the dip (0.1 to 1 ATR) and the close, buy the reclaim or the later quiet test, put the stop a few cents under the spring low, and take the stop as the trade, because a spring that fails usually fails at once. A single swing low is a 2B, a rising average is an undercut and rally, and a dip of 2 ATR or more is a breakdown.

questions.q: In Wyckoff's words, what is a spring?
choices: A quick dip under support, then back
A breakout over resistance that holds
A gap up on news over resistance
questions.answer: A quick dip under support, then back
questions.why: A quick dip under support, then back in. A spring takes price below the low of the range and reverses to close within it.
questions.lesson_line: A spring dips under the floor and snaps back inside.

wrong.A breakout over resistance that holds: That is a breakout. A spring goes under support, not over resistance.
wrong.A slow slide through support: A spring reverses quickly. Slower violations that fail are washouts or bear traps.
wrong.A gap up on news over resistance: A gap up is not a move under support.

questions.q: A spring takes price below the low of a range and then closes back inside the range.
questions.why: True. A spring takes price below the low of the range, then reverses and closes within it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the floor, then back inside the range.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A spring is bought at the floor on the ___ after the undercut.
questions.why: Reclaim. A spring is bought at the floor on the reclaim after the undercut, with the stop under the dip.
questions.lesson_line: Buy the reclaim at the floor, not the breakout at the top.

questions.q: Where in the range does a spring usually occur?
choices: On day one of the range
questions.why: Late in the range. Springs or shakeouts usually occur late within a range, and Fraser says the spring typically develops later in the formation.
questions.lesson_line: A spring comes late, after the range has had time to form.

wrong.On day one of the range: A floor has to form first. The spring comes late.
wrong.Only right after earnings: Nothing ties a spring to earnings. We avoid new buys near a report.
wrong.Before the range forms: Without a range there is no floor to dip under.

questions.q: The stop on a spring goes a few cents under the spring low.
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the spring low, the lowest low of the dip. Fraser also places stops under the low of the spring day.
questions.lesson_line: Stop a few cents under the spring low.

questions.q: How tall is a spring's range, floor to top?
questions.why: 6% to 20% from the floor to the top. Over 20% grades lower.
questions.lesson_line: A spring range is 6% to 20% tall.

wrong.1% to 3%: That is too tight to hold a real floor and a real top.
wrong.30% to 50%: Over 20% grades lower. This is far past it.
wrong.Any height will do: Height is one of the tests. Over 20% grades lower.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The spring dips at most about ___ ATR under the floor.
questions.why: 1. The day's low goes under the range's lowest low by at least 0.1 ATR and at most about 1 ATR.
questions.lesson_line: A real undercut, but no deeper than about 1 ATR.

questions.q: A dip of 3 ATR under the floor is still a spring.
questions.why: False. Over 2 ATR is a breakdown, not a spring. Fraser's number 1 spring is a complete breakdown and should not be bought.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2 ATR under the floor, it is a breakdown.

questions.q: What RS rating do we ask for in a spring?
questions.why: 80 or more. A spring is bought in a leader, stronger than the market through the range.
questions.lesson_line: A spring belongs to a leader, RS 80 or more.

wrong.20 or less: That is a weak stock. We want leaders for a spring.
wrong.About 50: An average stock is not a leader. The bar is 80.
wrong.None; any stock: The leader rule applies here. Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt.

questions.q: The reclaim day should close in the upper half of its range.
questions.why: True. Close quality matters: the reclaim day closes in the upper half of its range.
questions.lesson_line: A good reclaim closes in the upper half.

questions.q: Which market readings fit a spring?
choices: Red only, where we hold mostly cash
Orange only, where only A+ trades
questions.why: Green or Yellow. In an Orange market we take only A+ setups, and in a Red market we are mostly cash and shorts.
questions.lesson_line: Springs fit Green or Yellow markets.

wrong.Red only, where we hold mostly cash: In a Red market we are mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Orange only, where only A+ trades: In Orange we take only A+ setups, so it is not the home reading.
wrong.Any reading at all: The reading is a guide we follow, and springs fit Green or Yellow.

questions.q: What makes a range flat?
choices: Closes drift under a quarter of height
It makes a higher high every week
questions.answer: Closes drift under a quarter of height
questions.why: The closes drift less than a quarter of the range height. A flat range has no clear slope.
questions.lesson_line: Flat means no clear slope.

wrong.It makes a higher high every week: That is an uptrend, not a flat range.
wrong.It rises 20% in a month: That is a strong trend, not a flat range.
wrong.It trades on no volume: Flat describes price slope, not volume.

questions.q: A spring buy is fine two days before an earnings report.
questions.why: False. We take no new buy within 3 days of a report, and we skip on buyout news.
questions.lesson_line: No new buy within 3 days of a report.

questions.why: False. According to Wyckoff you should not buy breakouts. A breakout buy with the stop under the spring low had a median 12.5% stop.
questions.lesson_line: Do not buy the breakout. Buy at the floor.

questions.q: Floor 91.25, top 100.68. How tall is the range, in percent?
questions.why: 10.3%. (100.68 - 91.25) / 91.25. That sits inside the 6% to 20% band.
questions.lesson_line: Height is top minus floor, over the floor.

questions.q: The floor is 150.00, ATR is 3.00 and the spring low is 149.10. How deep is the dip, in ATR?
questions.why: 0.3 ATR. (150.00 - 149.10) / 3.00. That is a shallow dip, inside the 0.1 to about 1 ATR spring zone.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars under the floor, divided by the ATR.

questions.q: Fraser calls a shallow penetration of the prior low on modest volume what?
questions.why: A number 3 spring. Fraser says it can be bought immediately. A low-volume spring is also a good time to start a partial long.
questions.lesson_line: Shallow and quiet is the easiest spring to read.

wrong.A number 1 spring, a breakdown: A number 1 spring is a complete breakdown, and it should not be bought.
wrong.A test on high volume: A test comes after the spring, on lighter volume.
wrong.A breakout: A breakout goes over the top. A spring goes under the floor.

questions.q: A dip that is a complete breakdown on heavy volume should be bought as a spring.
questions.why: False. Fraser's number 1 spring is a complete breakdown, and it should not be bought. A close back under the spring low is not bought either.
questions.lesson_line: A breakdown on heavy volume is not a spring.

questions.q: Besides the floor, what does a spring often undercut?
choices: Nothing; it stays above all lines
questions.why: Under the 20-day or 50-day. The spring often undercuts those averages, but the stock must stay above the 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A spring can dip through the 20-day or 50-day. The 200-day stays intact.

wrong.The 200-day for good: No longs below the 200-day unless a parabolic long.
wrong.A new all-time low: A spring is a small dip under the floor, not a new low.
wrong.Nothing; it stays above all lines: The dip is under the floor, which often takes it under the shorter averages.

questions.q: Any dip under a recent low counts as a spring, even with no range behind it.
questions.why: False. A falling stock makes a new low every day. With no real range behind the dip, that is not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: No range, no spring.

questions.q: What is it?
choices: A spring in a flat range
questions.story: A stock rests in a flat 8-week range, 8% tall, with four touches of the floor. One day it dips 0.3 ATR under the floor and closes back inside, in the upper half of its range.
questions.answer: A spring in a flat range
questions.why: A spring. A flat range, a dip of 0.3 ATR and a close back inside in the upper half all fit.
questions.lesson_line: Flat range, shallow dip, strong close: a spring.

wrong.A breakdown: A breakdown goes over 2 ATR under the floor. This dip was 0.3 ATR.
wrong.A 2B of one low: A 2B has one swing low as its level. This floor has four touches.
wrong.A flat-base breakout: A breakout goes over the top. This stock dipped under the floor.

questions.q: Is this a spring?
choices: No; no range behind the dip
Yes; any undercut counts as one
questions.story: A stock makes a new low every day for two weeks. Then it ticks up and closes above yesterday's low.
questions.answer: No; no range behind the dip
questions.why: No. A falling stock makes a new low every day. With no real range behind the dip, that is not a spring.
questions.lesson_line: A spring needs a floor. A falling stock has none.

wrong.Yes; it closed back up: A bounce in a downtrend is not a spring. There is no floor to reclaim.
wrong.Yes; any undercut counts as one: A spring needs a flat range behind the undercut.
wrong.No; the volume is wrong: Volume is not the problem. The missing range is.

questions.q: Is this a spring?
choices: No; the dip was too slow
Yes; six days is a deep test
questions.story: A stock closes under its range floor for six sessions in a row, then closes back inside.
questions.answer: No; the dip was too slow
questions.why: No. A spring quickly reverses and moves back into the range. Slower violations that fail are washouts or bear traps.
questions.lesson_line: A spring snaps back. Six weak closes is not a snap.

wrong.Yes; it closed back inside: Closing back inside is part of it. The reversal also has to be quick.
wrong.Yes; six days is a deep test: A test comes after a spring. Six closes under is a slow violation.
wrong.Yes, with a smaller size: Size does not turn a slow violation into a spring.

questions.q: Spring, shakeout or breakdown?
choices: A U&R of a rising average
questions.story: The floor is 359.50. The dip goes 1.34 ATR under it, with one close under, then back inside the next day.
questions.why: A deeper shakeout; grade lower. Over 1 ATR is a shakeout and over 2 ATR is a breakdown. COST went 1.34 ATR and made 0.52R before it was stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Between 1 and 2 ATR deep, grade lower.

wrong.A clean spring: A clean spring dips about 1 ATR or less under the floor.
wrong.A breakdown; pass: A breakdown is over 2 ATR. This dip was 1.34 ATR.
wrong.A U&R of a rising average: The level here is a flat floor, not a rising average.

questions.q: Where does the stop go?
choices: No stop; it is a range
questions.story: The floor is 38.00. The spring low is 37.62. You buy the reclaim at 38.10.
questions.why: A few cents under 37.62, the spring low. The spring low is the real line, and the stop sits just under it.
questions.lesson_line: The stop goes under the spring low, not the old floor.

wrong.Right on 38.00, the old floor: The old floor is too tight. The spring low is the real line.
wrong.Far below, near 35.00: That is a wide stop, far past the spring low. The line is the spring low, a few cents under it.
wrong.No stop; it is a range: Every position has a real stop order with the broker.

questions.q: Study buy 171.85, stop 169.42. How far is the stop, in percent?
questions.why: 1.41%. (171.85 - 169.42) / 171.85. A stop a few cents under a shallow spring low is tight.
questions.lesson_line: Stop distance in percent is the gap over the entry.

questions.q: Buy the spring?
choices: Pass; springs need Green or Yellow
Yes; the stock itself is clean
Yes, at half size with a tight stop
questions.story: A clean spring in a stock above its 200-day. The market reading is Red.
questions.answer: Pass; springs need Green or Yellow
questions.why: Pass. Springs fit a Green or Yellow market, and this one is Red. GOOGL's spring failed in a market that was not Green.
questions.lesson_line: A clean spring in a Red market is still a pass.

wrong.Yes; the stock itself is clean: A clean chart does not beat the market reading.
wrong.Yes; springs ignore the market: They do not. Springs fit Green or Yellow readings.
wrong.Yes, at half size with a tight stop: Half size does not fix the wrong reading.

questions.q: What did the index tell you?
choices: Its own spring had not held
questions.story: A leader and QQQ both spring on the same day. Soon after, both are stopped out.
questions.answer: Its own spring had not held
questions.why: The index's own spring had not held. Wyckoff's step is to time your commitment with a turn in the index.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index. A failed index spring takes leaders with it.

wrong.Nothing; indexes do not matter: They do. The best springs come when the index has just sprung back.
wrong.The leader will bounce anyway: Both were stopped out. Hope is not a plan.
wrong.The spring was too shallow: Depth was not the problem. The index had not turned.

questions.q: What do you take from it?
choices: The setup is broken; quit it
questions.story: A 0.16 ATR dip on light volume in a 40-day range with three touches. A 1% stop. It is stopped on the entry day with no profit.
questions.why: A spring that fails usually fails at once. 41% broke their low before any test came. The stop under the spring low is the exit.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the trade, not a formality.

wrong.The setup is broken; quit it: One failed spring is the cost of the setup. 41% broke their low before any test.
wrong.The stop was too tight: The stop sat under the spring low, where it belongs.

questions.q: What do you do?
choices: Skip it; buyouts are off the list
Buy it; the shape is textbook perfect
Buy double; buyouts tend to jump
Buy it with a wide stop
questions.story: A textbook spring in a leader. Then a buyout report comes out.
questions.answer: Skip it; buyouts are off the list
questions.why: Skip it. We skip on buyout news. As soon as there is buyout stuff, it comes off the list.
questions.lesson_line: Buyout news takes the stock off the list.

wrong.Buy it; the shape is textbook perfect: A perfect shape does not beat the buyout rule.
wrong.Buy double; buyouts tend to jump: Size never goes up to chase a rumor.
wrong.Buy it with a wide stop: A wide stop does not fix the news risk.

questions.q: At entry, how far above its 10-day average may a stock be?
questions.why: No more than 10%. We skip a long more than 10% above its 10-day average.
questions.lesson_line: Too stretched above the 10-day means skip.

wrong.No more than 1%: That is far tighter than the rule.
wrong.There is no limit: There is a limit: 10% above the 10-day.

questions.q: What is wrong with that plan?
choices: The stop is far from the entry
questions.story: The scanner says to buy the range-top breakout and put the stop under the spring low.
questions.answer: The stop is far from the entry
questions.why: The stop is far from the entry. That plan had a median 12.5% stop and only 1% reached 3R. Wyckoff also says not to buy breakouts.
questions.lesson_line: Buy at the floor. A breakout buy leaves the stop far away.

wrong.The stop is too tight: It is the opposite. The stop sits far under a breakout entry.
wrong.Breakouts never work: Some do. The problem is the distance to the stop.
wrong.The range is too flat: A flat range is what we want.

questions.q: A spring still under 1R after 10 sessions is sold.
questions.why: True. Under 1R after 10 sessions, out.
questions.lesson_line: Ten sessions under 1R, sell.

questions.q: If a spring breaks its low, add to the position to average down.
questions.why: False. The stop under the spring low is the exit. It is the full size at one price with one stop, with no adding.
questions.lesson_line: A broken spring low means out, not more.

questions.q: What do you do at 3R?
choices: Sell a third at 148; stop to 142
questions.story: You bought at 142.00 with a stop at 140.00. Price reaches 148.00.
questions.answer: Sell a third at 148; stop to 142
questions.why: Sell a third at 3R, 148, and move the stop to breakeven at the first trim. Our plan expected a 3-1 gain by the breakout.
questions.lesson_line: A third at 3R, then the stop to breakeven.

wrong.Sell it all at 148: We sell a third at 3R and keep the rest working.
wrong.Hold everything for 160: A trim at 3R is the rule. Hoping for 160 skips it.
wrong.Add at 148: We never add. It is one price with one stop.

questions.q: How do we trail the rest of a spring?
choices: A fixed 3% stop under the entry
We never trail; we sell at the highs
questions.why: Under the 21-day for most springs, or the 10-day for fast movers, and out on a close below it.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the 21-day, or the 10-day when it runs.

wrong.Under the 200-day average line: The 200-day is far too slow to trail a spring.
wrong.A fixed 3% stop under the entry: A fixed stop does not follow the move.

questions.q: From a reclaim entry, about how far is the range top?
questions.why: About 4.8R in the median case, and 3R or more 72% of the time. So the 3R trim usually comes at or before the range top.
questions.lesson_line: The range top is the first resistance. The 3R trim comes first.

wrong.About 1R: The median is 4.8R, and 72% of the time it is 3R or more.
wrong.Right at the entry: The entry is at the floor. The top is the far side of the range.

questions.q: What now?
questions.story: You bought at 100.00 with a stop at 98.00. The stock gaps down and the first 30-minute low is 95.00.
questions.why: Out. On a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop, and a loss past 2R means get out.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is capped at 2R. Past that, leave.

wrong.Hold; it will bounce: The stop is the exit. Hope is not a plan.
wrong.Move the stop to 94.00: The stop only moves up, never wider.

questions.q: What do you do at the open?
choices: Sell the third at the open
Wait for 60.00 to sell the third
questions.story: You bought at 50.00 with a stop at 48.00. 3R is 56.00. The next day opens at 57.50.
questions.answer: Sell the third at the open
questions.why: Sell the third at the open. If a stock opens above a trim level, we take that trim at the open.
questions.lesson_line: If it opens past a trim level, sell at the open.

wrong.Wait for 60.00 to sell the third: A trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.
wrong.Hold everything and trail it: Holding it all risks giving the gap back.
wrong.Add at 57.50: We never add after a gap up. One price, one stop.

questions.q: Do the sources agree on volume at the spring?
choices: Yes; all of them want loud volume
questions.why: No. Fraser buys a spring on modest volume. Taylor says volume on the spring is typically quite high, the higher the better.
questions.lesson_line: The sources disagree on volume. Know both views.

wrong.Yes; all of them want loud volume: Fraser buys a spring on modest volume.
wrong.Yes; all want quiet volume: Taylor says volume on the spring is typically quite high.

questions.q: After a loud, deep spring, what does Fraser wait for?
choices: A test that makes a higher low
A gap up on heavy volume
The next earnings report to pass
questions.answer: A test that makes a higher low
questions.why: A test. High volume springs need to be tested in the following days or weeks. A successful test typically makes a higher low on lesser volume.
questions.lesson_line: After a loud spring, wait for the test.

wrong.A gap up on heavy volume: The sources wait for a test, not a gap.
wrong.The 200-day to turn upward: The line is not the test. The test is a pullback that holds above the spring low.
wrong.The next earnings report to pass: We avoid buying near a report, and it is not the test.

questions.q: Which range is the better place for a spring?
choices: A base after a long decline
A range right after an IPO
questions.why: A pause after a rise. The 60 sessions before the range rose, a reaccumulation pause, is preferred to a base after a decline.
questions.lesson_line: Prefer a pause after a rise to a base after a fall.

wrong.A base after a long decline: That is the classic accumulation spring. We prefer a pause after a rise.
wrong.A range under the 200-day: No longs under the 200-day unless a parabolic long.
wrong.A range right after an IPO: A new issue has no rise or floor history to read.

questions.q: Buy the spring?
questions.story: A textbook spring in a stock with an RS rating of 55, in a weak group.
questions.why: Skip. A spring is bought in a leader, RS 80 or more. Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt.
questions.lesson_line: No leader, no spring.

wrong.Buy; the shape is textbook: A textbook shape in a weak stock is still a pass.
wrong.Buy; springs are exempt: Only parabolic and mean-reversion trades are exempt from the leader rule.
wrong.Buy at half size: Size does not fix a weak stock.

questions.q: Buy, watch or pass?
choices: Buy now; it is a textbook spring
questions.story: A textbook spring under a flat 200-day, after a nine-month decline.
questions.why: Pass. We take no longs below the 200-day unless it is a parabolic long.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, a spring is a watch.

wrong.Buy now; it is a textbook spring: A textbook shape under the 200-day still breaks the rule.
wrong.Buy at half size: Half size does not fix a rule break.
wrong.Buy after a month: Time does not change the line. The stock must be back above it.

questions.q: How do you grade it?
choices: A+; a tall range is strong
Pass; it is not a spring
questions.story: A spring comes from a range 24% tall, with a dip of 1.4 ATR under the floor.
questions.why: Lower, on both counts. A range over 20% tall grades lower, and a dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout that grades lower.
questions.lesson_line: Tall range and deep dip both cost grade.

wrong.A+; the dip is shallow: 1.4 ATR is over the 1 ATR line, so it is not shallow.
wrong.Pass; it is not a spring: It is a spring, since 1.4 ATR is under 2, but it grades lower.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A Wyckoff spring in a range
questions.story: A stock undercuts its rising 50-day, with no flat range behind it, and closes back above the average.
questions.why: An undercut and rally. A U&R's level can be a rising average, one swing low or a prior high. A spring's floor is a flat level.
questions.lesson_line: A flat floor is a spring. A rising average is a U&R.

wrong.A Wyckoff spring in a range: A spring's floor is a flat level. A rising 50-day is not.
wrong.A capitulation flush: A capitulation is a straight fall with a 2 ATR flush. Nothing like that is here.
wrong.A flat base breakout: A flat base is bought through the top of a range.

questions.q: Name each trade.
questions.story: Two traders watch the same flat range. Trader A buys the reclaim at the floor. Trader B buys through the top.
questions.why: A buys a spring, at the floor on the reclaim, with the stop under the dip. B buys a flat base through the top, with the stop under the breakout day's low.
questions.lesson_line: Floor reclaim is a spring. Top breakout is a flat base.

wrong.A: flat base. B: spring: It is the other way round. The floor buy is the spring.
wrong.Both are springs: A spring is bought at the floor, not through the top.
wrong.Both are flat bases: A flat base is bought through the top, not at the floor.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: An Oops Reversal, not a spring
A spring; it undercut a low
questions.story: After a short dip with no range behind it, a stock breaks yesterday's low and reclaims yesterday's close on one candle.
questions.answer: An Oops Reversal, not a spring
questions.why: An Oops Reversal. It breaks yesterday's low and reclaims yesterday's close on one candle. A spring breaks the floor of a range.
questions.lesson_line: Yesterday's low is an Oops. The range floor is a spring.

wrong.A spring; it undercut a low: A spring undercuts the floor of a range. This was yesterday's low.
wrong.A capitulation: A capitulation is a 2 ATR flush on heavy volume.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base is bought through the top of a range.

questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A spring; it undercut a low
questions.story: A leader falls in a straight line. Then it drops 2.5 ATR in one day on twice the usual volume, under its 5, 9 and 20-day.
questions.why: A capitulation. A spring goes 0.1 to 1 ATR under the floor, and over 2 ATR is a breakdown. A 2 ATR flush on 2x volume is a capitulation.
questions.lesson_line: A big flush after a straight fall is a capitulation.

wrong.A spring; it undercut a low: A spring dips 0.1 to 1 ATR under a floor. This dropped 2.5 ATR.
wrong.A flat base: A flat base is bought through the top of a range.
wrong.An Oops Reversal: An Oops comes in an orderly pullback, not a 2.5 ATR flush.

questions.q: What do you do now?
choices: Log it; the stop was the trade
Move the stop under the next low
questions.story: You bought a spring in a 25-day range, 17.9% tall, after a 73% run. The same day it broke the spring low.
questions.answer: Log it; the stop was the trade
questions.why: Log it. The stop under the spring low is the exit, and a spring that fails usually fails at once. A new buy needs a new trigger.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-out is the cost of the setup.

wrong.Re-buy bigger at once: A new buy needs the setup to trigger again, as a new trade.
wrong.Move the stop under the next low: The stop only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Decide springs are broken: Some springs fail. That is why the stop sits under the spring low.

questions.q: Entry 142.00, stop 140.00, old range top 148.00. How many R is the top away?
questions.why: 3.0R. One R is 142.00 minus 140.00, or $2. The top is three times that above the entry. That matches the 3-1 gain the plan expected.
questions.lesson_line: Range top over the entry, divided by the risk.

questions.q: In our scan of 3,173 springs, about what share reached 3R before the stop?
questions.why: About a quarter: 27.1% reached 3R and 17.7% reached 5R, and 83.8% were stopped within the window. That is a fixed stop with no trims.
questions.lesson_line: A quarter got to 3R. The stop is the trade.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry, stop, first trim.
choices: Limit 23.30; stop 21.30; all at the top
questions.story: A flat shelf runs from 21.30 to 23.30 with four floor touches. A one-day dip to 21.25, 0.13 ATR under the floor, closes back inside. You buy at market, 21.43.
questions.why: Market 21.43; the stop a few cents under the spring low, 21.22; a third at 3R. GIS reached 23.8R at best.
questions.lesson_line: Entry at the reclaim, stop under the spring low, a third at 3R.

wrong.Limit 23.30; stop 21.30; all at the top: A limit at the ceiling is the breakout, and the stop sits under the spring low, not the old floor.
wrong.Market 21.43; stop 21.30; hold a month: A stop on the old floor is too tight. The spring low is the real line.

questions.q: Hidden ticker. The last bar undercut a recent low and closed back above it. Take it or pass?
choices: Take it; flat floor, modest dip
Pass; there is no range behind it
Pass; the dip is a real breakdown
questions.answer: Take it; flat floor, modest dip
questions.why: Take it. A flat range 7.2% tall, five floor touches, and one probe of 0.75 ATR that closed back inside on 0.96x volume.
questions.lesson_line: A flat floor and a modest dip that snaps back.

wrong.Pass; there is no range behind it: Look again: the floor was touched five times.
wrong.Pass; the dip is a real breakdown: A breakdown is over 2 ATR. This probe was 0.75 ATR.

questions.q: Hidden ticker. The last bar undercut an old low and closed back above it. Spring or pass?
choices: Pass; one swing low is a 2B
Take it; the dip is shallow
Take it; the floor is flat
questions.answer: Pass; one swing low is a 2B
questions.why: Pass. One swing low, 40 sessions old, set the floor, and price rallied 14% off it. That is a 2B, not a spring: there is no flat range to look left at.
questions.lesson_line: A single low is a 2B. A spring needs a flat floor.

wrong.Take it; the dip is shallow: A shallow dip does not make a floor. A spring needs a flat range.
wrong.Take it; the floor is flat: The floor is one low, not a flat level touched more than once.

questions.q: What does Wyckoff's step 5 ask of the buyer?
choices: Time your buy with a turn in the index
questions.answer: Time your buy with a turn in the index
questions.why: Time your commitment with a turn in the stock market index. Springs work best when the index itself has just sprung back.
questions.lesson_line: Wait for the index to turn.

wrong.Buy before the index turns: Step 5 says to time your buy with the turn, not ahead of it.
wrong.Ignore the index: The index matters. A failed index spring takes leaders with it.
wrong.Buy only on a Monday: Nothing in the step mentions a weekday.

questions.q: Taylor says the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree.
questions.why: True. In his view the spring low should not be violated by any significant degree, or the structure is invalidated.
questions.lesson_line: A spring that breaks its low is invalid.

questions.q: Pruden calls the spring the first place to buy. What does he say is better?
questions.why: The later secondary test. Pruden says the spring is the first prescribed place to buy and the secondary test is better.
questions.lesson_line: A quiet test can beat the spring itself.

wrong.The breakout over the top: Wyckoff says not to buy breakouts.
wrong.The selling climax: The test comes after the spring, not at a climax.
wrong.Waiting a year: The test comes in the following days or weeks.

questions.q: Which candidate grades higher?
choices: A; the range, dip and close are cleaner
B; the deeper dip shook out more
questions.story: A: a range 8% tall, a dip of 0.3 ATR, a reclaim that closes in the upper half. B: a range 24% tall, a dip of 1.4 ATR, a reclaim that closes mid-range.
questions.answer: A; the range, dip and close are cleaner
questions.why: A. A range over 20% tall grades lower. A dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout that grades lower. A good reclaim closes in the upper half.
questions.lesson_line: Short range, shallow dip, strong close: the higher grade.

wrong.B; the deeper dip shook out more: A dip over 1 ATR is a shakeout, and it grades lower.
wrong.They grade the same: Range height, dip depth and close quality all separate them.
wrong.Neither; both are breakdowns: A breakdown is over 2 ATR. Neither dip is that deep.

questions.q: How does that change the setup?
choices: It is weaker; the index is irrelevant
It is a pass; the index must lead
It is a pass; Green is for shorts
questions.story: A leader springs in a flat range. The index sprang back from a correction last week, and the market reading is Green.
questions.why: It is stronger. A spring is best when the index itself has just sprung back, and Green or Yellow readings fit a spring.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's spring with a turning index is the best case.

wrong.It is weaker; the index is irrelevant: The index matters. Wyckoff says to time your buy with a turn in the index.
wrong.It is a pass; the index must lead: We ask only that the index has just sprung back.
wrong.It is a pass; Green is for shorts: Green or Yellow is the reading for a spring.

questions.q: Which range is the better spring base?
choices: A; a pause after a rise
B; a base after a fall
questions.story: Range A follows a 31% rise. Range B follows a 13% fall. Both are flat, 12% tall, and above the 200-day.
questions.answer: A; a pause after a rise
questions.why: A. The 60 sessions before the range should have risen, a reaccumulation pause, not a base after a decline. HWM was a stepping stone after a 31% run.
questions.lesson_line: Prefer a pause after a rise to a base after a fall.

wrong.B; a base after a fall: A base after a decline is the less preferred prior trend.
wrong.They are equal: The prior trend separates them. A rise is preferred.

questions.q: When does the stop go to breakeven on a spring?
choices: At the first trim, by default
questions.answer: At the first trim, by default
questions.why: At the first trim by default, and anywhere between 2R and 5R. A third comes off at 3R.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes with the first trim.

wrong.Never: The stop moves to breakeven between 2R and 5R.
wrong.Before the buy: There is no position yet. Breakeven comes after the first trim.
wrong.At the open each day: The stop only moves up when the rule says so, not each day.

questions.q: What type is this, and what next?
choices: A number 2 spring; wait for the test
questions.story: The dip goes much further under the low on expanded volume. Then it lifts briefly and drops back toward the lows.
questions.answer: A number 2 spring; wait for the test
questions.why: A number 2 spring. It goes further below the low on expanded volume, then lifts and drops back for a test. High volume springs need to be tested first.
questions.lesson_line: A deeper, louder spring waits for its test.

wrong.A number 3 spring; buy now: A number 3 spring is shallow on modest volume. This one is deeper and louder.
wrong.A number 1 spring; buy now: A number 1 spring is a complete breakdown, and it should not be bought.
wrong.A breakout; add: The stock dipped under the low. A breakout goes over the top.

questions.q: Four valid springs lost. Which one had no warning sign?
choices: TSLA; a tall range after a run
questions.why: MSFT. It met every rule and was stopped on the entry day. GOOGL's market, AAPL's index and TSLA's 17.9% range after a 73% run were warnings.
questions.lesson_line: Some good springs still fail. The stop is the trade.

wrong.GOOGL; the market was weak: It was not a Green market, a warning sign.
wrong.AAPL; the index failed: QQQ sprang the same day and failed too, a warning sign.
wrong.TSLA; a tall range after a run: A 17.9% range after a 73% run was a warning sign.

conflicts: UNIT ID IS PROVISIONAL: UNITS-method.md has no row for this card (the card's unit is 'none'). SET.50 and the skill id setup.wyckoff_spring are built from the criteria card and its dossier alone and wait on the setup map (D-002: the dossier and the register lean to a named variant inside U&R under a flat base, taught as a U&R) and the names (UCT never says 'Wyckoff spring' in public; its words are shakeout, failed breakdown and UnR).

Pending-owner criteria kept OUT of every key (our current default, waiting on the owner): spr.above_200 as a spring-specific rule (D-009; q19, q42 and q44 key only the settled B26 line, no longs under the 200-day unless a parabolic long, and the card's 'must stay above the 200-day' sentence is not quoted); spr.range_length, 20 sessions against the app's 15 (D-112; no range length is keyed, and the NFLX 2025-09-15 near-miss of a 19-session range is not used); spr.floor_touches, two swing lows at least 5 sessions apart (D-112; the stories give touch counts as givens, and the only touch rule keyed is that one old swing low is a 2B, q55, which fails every option); spr.reclaim_window, the same day or the next (D-005; nothing keys 'one-bar' or 'two-bar' as a rule, the INTC 2005-08-29 near-miss of 3 closes under is not used, q23 keys only Pruden's 'quickly reverses' and Taylor's 'slower violations'); spr.volume, quiet under 1.0x and loud 1.5x or more (D-006; q40 teaches the sources' disagreement and q17 and q41 teach Fraser's types as his, never a cutoff); spr.entry_reclaim and spr.entry_test, which entry we teach (D-003; q03 keys 'buy the reclaim at the floor' as the card's lookalike tell against the flat base, and q41 and q59 key the test as the Wyckoff school's, never as ours); spr.no_chase, 4% over the old range low (D-004/D-113; no item); spr.stop_width, 3% and 5% bands (D-022; only the arithmetic of a stop distance is asked, q26); the upthrust short, whether to teach it, the warning only, or drop it (D-001; no item names the upthrust or a short).

Settled and proposed criteria are keyed: spr.leader (C31, RS 80), spr.liquidity, spr.earnings_window (B22), spr.market_reading (F65), spr.stop (A3, F62), spr.stop_gap (B20), spr.trim_1, spr.breakeven, spr.trim_2, spr.trim_gap_open, spr.trail, spr.time_stop (C33), spr.not_stretched (C29), spr.after_entry_stop; and the proposed spr.prior_advance, spr.index_sprung, spr.range_height, spr.flat, spr.dip_depth (0.1 to 1 ATR, 1 to 2 ATR grades lower, over 2 ATR a breakdown), spr.reclaim_close, spr.location_averages, spr.not_breakout_entry, spr.range_top_resistance, spr.inv_no_range, spr.inv_close_under_low. Every question keyed on them carries house: true except the two-publisher items (q01, q02, q04, q17, q23, q40, q41, q59, and the Fraser items q64), and the owner's review is the gate. The ranges (6% to 20%, a quarter of the height, 0.1 to 1 ATR) are the dossier's own proposals, marked 'my proposal' there; no source publishes a number for a spring.

The unit separates the spring from U&R, 2B, the flat base, Oops and Capitulation by the card's tells that carry no pending number: a flat floor against one swing low (2B, q55), a flat floor against a rising average or a prior high (U&R, q46), the floor buy against the top buy (flat base, q47), the range floor against yesterday's low (Oops, q48), the 0.1 to 1 ATR dip against a 2 ATR flush (Capitulation, q49). The numbers those tells carry for the OTHER cards (the 2B's 1 ATR rally, the U&R's 3 sessions, the Oops range under 3 ATR, the Remount's 5 closes) are left out of every quote and key.

Sources: the Pruden, ChartSchool, Fraser and Taylor quotes are the dossier's section 3 quotes. The Pruden and von Lichtenstein paper (s2) is a PDF, and the PDF text extraction drops spaces in places, so two Pruden lines ('springs or shakeouts usually occur late' and 'an upthrust is the opposite of a spring') are not quoted; w01, w03, w04 and w05 are matched by the quote checker. Fraser's two StockCharts posts (s3, s4) are one author on one site, so they never count as two publishers; the UCT items (u01 to u04) are public Substack quotes in the owner's own Sunday Scans section, cited as Tier 3 house sources with their public URLs. The DELL math (u01 to u03) is the owner's only written spring plan; it uses a stop at $140, the shakeout low, not 'a few cents under' it, and q35 and q51 use it only for the 3R arithmetic and the 3-1 gain the plan expected.

Volume is the sources' biggest disagreement (Fraser, Pruden and ChartSchool want a quiet spring and a test after a loud one; Taylor wants heavy volume, the higher the better). q40 asks only whether they agree, and the answer is no; our own use of volume is D-006 and is not taught. The dossier's measurement found no separation on daily bars.

The dossier's example numbers (d1) are a Tier 3 repo source: read off our own daily bars by the research scan (dossier sections 13 and 14), survivors only, fixed stop three cents beyond the probe's extreme, no RS rating or group applied; the owner has not reviewed the examples. The walk-throughs (GIS, HWM, MSFT) and the chart questions (q54 ODFL asof 2021-10-01, the spring day; q55 AMZN asof 2021-08-12, the day of the probe) depend on it. The chart ends on the spring day, so 'take it' means 'this is a spring worth the plan', not an order at that bar. The buy in the scan is the next open, usually worse than the intraday reclaim.

KMX 2020-12-29 (a two-bar spring) is not used because the one-bar and two-bar windows are D-005; the AAPL 2014, ULTA, PH, AVGO and GS/TGT upthrust examples are not used either (AVGO and PH have 2 floor touches, which D-112 may raise; the upthrusts are D-001). The four failures kept are GOOGL (market), AAPL 2021 (the index's own spring), MSFT (fails at once) and TSLA (a 17.9% tall range after a 73% run); MSFT and TSLA are asked as 'what do you do' items, GOOGL and AAPL as market and index lessons.

q35, q38 and q39 use the house trim, gap and breakeven rules (B19, B20, F63) with stated prices; q35's calc proves 148 = 142 + 3 x 2 and q38's calc proves the 2.5R loss. The base rate in q52 (27.1% to 3R, 17.7% to 5R, 83.8% stopped) is a fixed-stop, no-trim measurement of the scan's springs, not the house trade.

Cold check 2026-11-10: 52 pass (15 fixed), 0 fix, 15 cut; the three things the owner should look at first: (1) the name and home (D-002): UCT says shakeout, failed breakdown and UnR in public, never 'Wyckoff spring', and the register leans to a named variant inside U&R; (2) D-003: q47 and the walk-throughs key buying the reclaim at the floor as the card's tell (the entry we teach is pending); (3) the dossier's example notes disagree with the bars in two places (MSFT 'never showed a profit', TSLA 'never traded above the entry'), so the dossier's failure table needs a recheck before it is used elsewhere. Publisher decision: StockCharts ChartSchool (Bogomazov and Lipsett) and Fraser's two articles are all on stockcharts.com, so they count as one publisher; q04 and q17 rested on that miscount and now add Pruden (w06, w07) as the independent second source; Pruden and Taylor (CMT) stay separate publishers. Upthrust and short material: none in the unit. No sizing question; A7's 40% cap does not arise.
